title: Democrats in striking distance: New CNN polls in four states highlight party’s path to Senate majority
content: CNN polling across four key Senate races in the final days of the midterm campaign finds Democrats well-positioned in Michigan and Texas , with no clear leader in the races in Maine or Kansas . The four states tell the story of a midterm playing field that has shifted in unexpected ways, leaving Democrats hopeful that they’ll be able to take control of the Senate after next Tuesday’s elections. That prospect largely seemed out of reach earlier this year, and it remains far from a done deal. But with President Donald Trump’s ratings underwater even in states he won easily in 2024, territory that was once staunchly Republican now appears to be up for grabs. In Michigan, the epitome of a battleground state, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed (49%) has opened up a lead over Republican Mike Rogers (42%) among likely voters amid signs that the state’s Democratic base has unified behind him, and that discouraged Republicans are checking out. Texas, which hasn’t elected a Democrat in a statewide race in three decades, gives Democrat James Talarico (49%) a narrow lead over Republican Ken Paxton (43%) among likely voters. Talarico’s bid benefits from deeply negative impressions of Paxton, as well as sizable support among the Black, Latino and Asian voters in the state who voted for Trump in 2024. Early on, Maine was widely viewed as one of Democrats’ best pickup opportunities this cycle, with Sen. Susan Collins the only Republican up for reelection in a state that voted Democratic in 2024. But the race has remained a tight contest: The new poll of likely voters finds no clear leader between Collins (45%) and her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson (49%), even as the race has become squarely a referendum on Collins. And in deep-red Kansas, there is no clear leader between Democrat Adam Hamilton (49%) and Republican Sen. Roger Marshall (45%), even as likely voters there say they would prefer Republicans to control the Senate. Voters here largely view Marshall unfavorably and say their choices are about Marshall more so than Hamilton. Taken together, these four states paint a picture of a Democratic Party well-positioned to make a play for Senate control. They exemplify the extraordinary range of the playing field in a political environment that borders on historic negativity toward the party in power, and of the ways in which individual candidates can overcome – or succumb to – the forces of political habit. For Democrats to take control of the Senate, they will need a net gain of four seats; three of these four seats are currently held by Republicans. Beyond the core math, they’ll need the prevailing political winds and the dynamics of these individual races to align. There is still room for those dynamics to shift. In all but Maine, at least 1 in 8 likely voters say they could still change their mind about whom to support. In Texas and Kansas, at least 6 in 10 of those uncommitted likely voters are Republicans or Republican-leaning independents, suggesting there is room for political gravity to work in the GOP’s favor as voters settle on their decisions. More than 9 in 10 Maine likely voters, though, say they are locked into their choice. In all four states, enough voters are movable to close the gap between candidates. El-Sayed has opened up a lead over Rogers in what was a no-clear-leader race in CNN’s polling around Labor Day . That lead rests on worsening views of Rogers, as well as consolidated support among Democrats following the state’s contentious August primary. All told, El-Sayed now holds the support of 95% of Democratic likely voters, up a touch from 90% in the last poll. Likely voters in the state are largely making their choices based on their views of El-Sayed. Three-quarters of his supporters see their vote as one of support for him, and 57% of Rogers supporters say their vote is against El-Sayed – a reversal in how Rogers’ voters view their choice compared with earlier in the campaign. That shift comes as views of Rogers have notably worsened: 50% now have an unfavorable view of the former Congressman, up from 42% in early September. El-Sayed’s favorable ratings remain roughly evenly split between positive and negative views. Texas’ tilt toward a Democrat in its Senate contest demonstrates how individual candidates can short - circuit political currents. Trump carried Texas in 2024 by the largest margin in any of his three runs for the presidency, winning over sizable shares of the state’s voters of color, including a majority of Latino and Asian voters. And there are signs that Talarico, to a greater extent than some other Democratic candidates, is overperforming the political environment. Talarico has the support of 63% of Latino likely voters in the state and 64% among likely voters of color generally. That includes carrying 22% of likely voters of color who say they backed Trump in 2024. Talarico’s favorability rating is far more positive than Paxton’s, and most Talarico supporters say their decision is more of a sign of support for the Democrat than an anti-Paxton vote. The poll finds Paxton struggling to generate positive support even among his own partisans: 24% hold an unfavorable view of Paxton, compared with just 2% of Democrats holding a negative view of Talarico. Still, nobody would confuse Texas for being Democratic-friendly territory. While Trump’s approval rating in the state has tipped into the negative, the GOP remains more popular than the Democratic Party, and there’s no clear leader in the state’s race for governor. In Kansas, the most Republican-friendly of the four states polled, only about one-third hold a positive view of the Democratic Party. But Hamilton, like Talarico, is overperforming his party – even as he’s a lesser-known quantity. In this case, the more relevant number may be Marshall’s underperformance and unpopularity. Most likely voters say that they view the Republican nominee negatively, and a 59% majority of Hamilton’s backers say they’re motivated primarily by opposition to Marshall. Hamilton has the support of roughly 12% of Republican and Republican-leaning voters, a significantly broader crossover than for any other Democratic candidate tested. And those voters without an opinion of Hamilton – about one-fifth of the electorate – still support him over Marshall. There is no clear leader in the Maine Senate race, and the fundamentals of the race remain roughly the same as in CNN’s last poll there just ahead of Labor Day. Collins’ continued competitive position speaks to her ability to defray criticism that she is too close to an unpopular president. Compared to GOP nominees in the other three states, Collins is less broadly seen as willing to place the interests of Trump and the Republican Party ahead of the people in her state. In fact, Maine likely voters are about as apt to see Jackson as beholden to the Democratic Party as they are to say Collins is to the GOP. Collins also picks up more support among Trump disapprovers (21%) than any of the other GOP candidates tested in these polls (Rogers at 16%, Marshall at 12%, Paxton at 10%). Collins needs to win over some voters dissatisfied with her party, because views of the GOP are more negative in Maine than in any of the other states polled. The race is clearly turning on views of Collins herself. About three-quarters of likely voters behind each candidate say their choices are motivated by Collins more than Jackson. Her favorability rating remains broadly net-negative (54% have an unfavorable view), but Jackson’s is also narrowly negative (46% unfavorable to 39% favorable). And many more report seeing advertising in support of Collins (42%) than of Jackson (27%). In the final stretch, the poll finds that while Jackson’s backers remain more motivated to vote (79% are extremely motivated compared with 62% among Collins’ supporters), deep motivation among Collins’ voters has grown by 9 points since early September while motivation among Jackson’s voters has held steady. Many voters across these four states are keenly aware that their choice carries national implications. For some, that’s a driving factor – even beyond the character of the candidates and the issues at play in the specific races. A 55% majority of the voters supporting the Democrat Jackson in Maine say that party control is their top concern, while in Texas and Kansas, it’s more of a factor for those backing Republican candidates than Democrats, including being the top consideration for half of those supporting Marshall in Kansas. But in these states that are likely to be central to determining who holds power in the Senate next year, a majority of voters point to other factors as their top consideration. CNN’s Isabelle LaBianco contributed to this report.
ranking_reason: Democrats in striking distance: New CNN polls in four states highlight party’s path to Senate majority

analysis.reason: Democrats in striking distance: New CNN polls in four states highlight party’s path to Senate majority

final_quality.reason: The article provides new, evidence-based information about the current state of the midterm elections, specifically highlighting the Democrats' chances of taking control of the Senate in four key states. The polling data provides a clear reason for readers to care, as it indicates a shift in the political landscape and a potential upset in traditionally Republican strongholds.

title: Student-backed election winners demand sweeping resignations in Serbia
content:
Serbia's victorious student-led movement has called for top figures in the police, intelligence and judiciary to stand down, days after ousting ex-president Aleksandar Vučić's party from power.
Standing in Pioneers' Park opposite parliament, newly elected MPs on the Student List demanded the immediate dismissal of all police officers who had broken the law, singling out the heads of the police, the BIA security agency and anti-terror unit.
It is not often a European country votes to fully reset its political system overnight, and Serbians have voted to hand the task to a group of novice politicians, made up of intellectuals, professors, artists, athletes and as many as 12 medical doctors and surgeons.
But the handover of power will take weeks, and the students' movement is concerned that evidence of possible wrongdoing could be destroyed in that time.
Just a few days ago, the park they were standing in on Thursday was a tent camp, filled with Vučić loyalists outside his office.
Within hours of him admitting defeat on Sunday night, the camp was dismantled, and a team of volunteers moved in on Monday morning to clean up the mess.
"This is just the first wave of spring cleaning, the new ones are coming now - we are very excited but ready to do it too," said Marija Milovanović, 25, as she scrubbed a park bench.
The student movement emerged from protests following the fatal collapse of a railway station canopy that killed 16 people in November 2024, in Serbia's second largest town Novi Sad.
Their desire was to bring those responsible to justice, and investigate widespread corruption claims blamed for one of the most tragic events in Serbia's modern history.
They have made some bold promises.
Under their Student Plan, they promise to "halt the plunder, return stolen goods to the state budget, and invest directly in education and the economy".
The purge of Vučić loyalists has already begun at Serbia's state broadcaster RTS, where director Manja Grčić has stepped down.
Newly elected MP Mirjana Nikolić said Serbian citizens had the right to truthful information and RTS had served the interests of the government for years.
The new MPs have also set their sights on replacing the head of Telekom Srbija, Vladimir Lučić.
Vučić loyalist Ana Brnabić, who is currently Serbia's acting president, has accused her opponents of choosing "revolutionary justice, not rule of law," and of aiming to shut down "all of the media they dislike".
But one of the next government's best-known MPs, Dejan Šoškić, argues that key reforms need to be in place fast.
"In the first six months, I would like to see the media scene liberated, fighting against corruption on the way, the institutions operating as prescribed by laws and a lustration law introduced," said Šoškić, an economist who served as governor of the central bank between 2010 and 2012.
By lustration, he means banning from public office members of the Vučić government or party apparatus who are found to have violated the rights of Serbians.
That kind of purge will take time, as all of Serbia's main pillars of authority have been held by Vučić and his party for so long, warns Strahinja Subotić of Belgrade-based European Policy Centre.
Ultimately, he believes the new administration will have to "build bridges to the segments that have been operating well in the past".
ranking_reason: Serbian students' movement demands sweeping resignations in police, intelligence, and judiciary, calling for a reset of the political system overnight.

analysis.reason: Serbian students' movement demands sweeping resignations in police, intelligence, and judiciary, calling for a reset of the political system overnight.

final_quality.reason: This article reports a substantive and important development in the category of people, specifically in the context of a significant political shift in Serbia, with a clear reason for readers to care, as it highlights the impact of the students' movement on the country's political system and the promises they have made to bring about change.

title: Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of trying to 'delegitimise' election
content:
The main Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and Arab-led party leaders have denounced Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleging foreign interference following the election which saw his coalition lose its majority.
Netanyahu's Likud accused Israel's Arab-led parties of "stealing" the election. Home security agency Shin Bet is investigating whether they received illegal funding from Qatar and Turkey.
Qatar's foreign ministry denied the "ridiculous and dangerous" allegations and accused Israeli politicians of conducting a disinformation campaign against Doha.
Final results confirmed that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition had won a majority in parliament.
The two Arab party lists - The Joint List and the Ra'am - defied expectations to win a record 19 seats in the 120-seat Knesset following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That positions them as potential kingmakers, with Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats and his rival Gadi Eisenkot's bloc securing 48.
On Thursday Likud alleged that voters had been "bribed" to vote for Arab parties, after the head of the Central Elections Committee (CEC) asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate "serious suspicions" of foreign interference.
Both Arab parties strongly rejected the claim, with the Arab-majority Joint List alliance saying it was baseless.
The row is being seen by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to delegitimise the Arab parties, thereby making it politically impossible for Eisenkot to join forces with them - which is currently his bloc's only route to power.
Israeli media reported that the CEC had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's Foreign Ministry "categorically" denied the claims.
Netanyahu and his Likud Party framed the allegations as a "political earthquake" and an "an attack on democracy", aimed at removing their right-wing government.
But the Shin Bet later clarified that their investigation did not implicate an entire community who had voted legally, while acting CEC Director General Dean Livne said there was "no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity."
Eisenkot, who was briefed on the investigation, said "it is too early to determine what happened, or if anything happened at all," and accused Netanyahu of running "an orchestrated and organized campaign to delegitimize the election results".
Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, who is part of the Joint List, dismissed the allegation, saying: "The losing side is constructing a racist blood libel and calling on the security agencies to use force in order to overturn the election results."
Netanyahu's attacks on Arab voters and parties have been ongoing for days. He spent much of election day posting on social media that high Arab turnout is an "emergency" and a "matter of life or death" for the Israeli right. He also shared AI-generated images of Arab voters at polling stations, in an attempt to encourage right-wingers to get out and vote.
Arab Israelis, many of whom refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up about one fifth of the country.
For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout on Tuesday was inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, led by Netanyahu.
The final results offer only three plausible options for a government to be formed: a national unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.
Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but speculation has swirled in recent days that an agreement could yet be reached.
A snap poll conducted by Hebrew University showed that the most popular option for voters from every party in the opposition bloc was for Eisenkot to form a minority government with Ra'am, and supported from outside by the Joint List.
ranking_reason: The article reports a meaningful, substantive development relevant to its category.

analysis.reason: The article reports a meaningful, substantive development relevant to its category.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a significant development in Israeli politics, shedding light on the controversy surrounding Netanyahu's allegations of foreign interference and its potential impact on the political landscape. The piece provides a clear reason for readers to care, as it highlights the potential implications for the country's political future and the role of Arab-led parties in Israeli politics.
